TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation
2.1 The Committee notes the efforts of the Department towards settlement of pending UCs and
hopes that pendency of UCs would not be a hindrance in the successful implementation of these
schemes/projects. (Para 2.11)
Action Taken
2.2 The recommendation of the Hon’ble Committee has been noted for compliance.
III INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH (ICMR)
Recommendation
2.3 The Committee is of the view that ICMR needs to focus more on  such research areas wherein
the country is witnessing high disease burden. The thrust areas may be identified by ICMR which
the students of MD/MS may select from so that the research outcomes are relevant in prevention
as well as cure of certain diseases. Awarding financial assistance to these students would certainly
incentivize the orientation of students towards research. The Committee recommends that concerted
efforts need to be made to encourage students for undertaking research projects and there is need
to inculcate research vigour that may generate research leads, the fruits of which can be translated
into tangible outcomes. (Para 3.17)
Action Taken
2.4
z The ICMR is already pursuing Postgraduate programmes through recognized medical
institutions, One such scheme is “MD/MS/DM/MCH/MDS Thesis- Financial Support”
primarily aimed at promoting good quality research amongst medical college students
pursuing post-graduation courses as well as to improve visibility and accessibility of
their research work to larger research audience in the country. The  applications  are
invited  twice a year on June 30th and December 31st.
z ICMR provides financial assistance of ` 50,000/ to selected candidates pursuing  postgraduate
courses (MD/MS/ MCH). Number of awards is limited to 100 per year (No. of Awards
for MDS course is limited to 10%). The Eligibility criteria for the  same is that Medical
graduates who are admitted to the Post-graduation course (MCI/DCI recognized) in
Institute/College and who wish to avail ICMR award/financial assistance for pursuing
their research project can apply under this scheme. The Upper age limit is 45 years of
age and tenure of fellowship is for three and half years.
z ICMR has already specifically included the thrust areas for the above program to be
undertaken, mainly, Anti-Microbial Resistance  (AMR), Tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS Malaria,
Diabetes, Maternal and Child health.
3

4
z The MD/MS/DM/ MCH/ MDS Thesis- Financial Support primarily aims and encourages
the Post-graduate Medical Students to undertake research topics in the above mentioned
areas specifically, research outcomes of which can be used for translating them into
products useful for the country.

CHAPTER - III
 RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE
GOVERNMENT HA VE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation
3.1 The Committee observes that constraints of funds should not come in the way of the medical
as well as health research. The Committee would like the Department to formulate a Comprehensive
Action Plan, while projecting its funds requirement before the Ministry of Finance. The Committee
believes that the Department of Health Research has not been effective in persuading the Ministry
of Finance for seeking required funds and therefore, the additional funds are received   at fag end
of the Financial Year . The Committee recommends that the Department should be more proactive
in holding pre- budget discussion and forwarding the proposals for Supplementary Grant in order
to ensure that funds are released well in advance at RE stage. (Para 2.3)
Action Taken
3.2 The recommendation of the Hon’ble Committee has been noted for compliance. Necessary
action would be taken by the Department to more effectively project its requirements before the
Ministry of Finance during pre-budgetary discussions on finalization of the Revised Estimates for
2018-19.
Further Recommendation
3.3 The Committee believes that the Department of Health Research had effectively forwarded
its requirements of funds at the stage of Revised Estimate for 2018-19 to complete the
schemes of DHR and ICMR as per the set targets. However, the Committee would like to
be apprised of the funds received at RE stage and the physical achievement of ongoing/
already sanctioned projects against the set targets. The Committee also believes that DHR
would also hold budget discussion  2019-20 with Ministry of Finance and effectively place  its
projected demand as per Comprehensive Action Plan, as noted by DHR in Para 2.3 of  107th
Report for compliance. In this regard, the Committee would like to be apprised of the
ingredients of Comprehensive Action Plan of DHR and the requirement of funds to accomplish
the set objectives/targets.
Recommendations
3.4 The Committee notes while on the one hand the Department claims that here is shortfall of
funds for implementation of the projects/schemes of the Department on the other hand, there is
under-utilization of funds with respect to certain schemes/projects like Development of Tools to
prevent Outbreaks of epidemics (33.20%); Human Resource Development for Health Research
(53.15%), Grant-in-aid Scheme for inter-sectoral convergence and Coordination for Promotion &
Guidance on Health Research (55.43%),  Research Governance–HTA (6.83%), International Cooperation
(14.00%), Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) 69.68%), Secretariat Expenditure  (60.71).
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should seriously monitor the funds
allocated at BE stage as well as RE stage in each quarter with a view to ensure optimum
5

6
utilization of resources. The Committee also recommends that Department must explore innovative
solutions, prepare flexible and workable action plan, aimed to meet all deadlines and develop
strategic  alternatives  wherever the current strategy may not yield the intended results so as to
accomplish the physical and financial targets. (Para 2.5)
Action Taken
3.5 As a result of the vigorous efforts made by the Department, The actual expenditure achieved
upto 31.3.2018 is `1731.68 crores, against the RE allocation of `1743.39 crores, which is about
99.28% of the RE allocation. The scheme-wise position is given in Annexure-I.
3.6 Meetings are held on weekly/fortnightly basis to review the physical and financial progress
of the schemes/projectsand for taking necessary measures to ensure optimum utilization of allocated
funds. Department is also actively deliberating on how to bring in functional integration between
DHR and ICMR for efficient management & implementation of schemes/programmes; utilizing the
technical support from ICMR for achieving requisite outcomes from the various schemes and use
of information technology for monitoring the performance of schemes.
Further Recommendation
3.7 The Committee notes the measures taken by DHR to ensure the optimum utilisation
of allocated funds on various schemes, although adequate appropriation of funds at BE
Stage, itself would ensure execution of schemes as per originally conceived time frame and
not at the fag end/last quarter of financial year. That would also ensure compliance of
guideline of the Ministry of Finance as regards streamlining  and even further expenditure
throughout the financial year.
3.8 The Committee would like to be apprised of the outcome of the measures taken for
financial integration between DHR and ICMR and the outcome of the efforts so undertaken
for better/efficient management and implementation of the scheme/programmes.
Recommendation
3.9 The Committee observes that the Department of Health Research is mandated to promote
basic, applied and clinical research related to medical health and biomedical performance in
cutting edge areas. Starving of the on-going and proposed basic, applied and clinical research
projects in the medical and public health research would prove detrimental to generation of new
knowledge in the areas of health research. The Committee, therefore, lends its support for enhancement
of funds to the tune of 454.58 crore to the Department of Health Research for financial year
2018-19. The Department of Health Research must take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance.
The Committee desires to be apprised of response of the Ministry of Finance in this regard. The
Committee also recommends that a robust monitory mechanism should be put in place for proper
utilization of allocated funds through financial management to ensure that the schemes does not
get sidetracked due to lack of funds. (Para 2.8)
Action Taken
3.10 The Department appreciates the recommendations and support of the Hon’ble Committee for
enhancement of allocation for 2018-19. Necessary action would be taken by the Department to

7
project its requirements before the Ministry of Finance more effectively with proper justification
and details during pre-budgetary discussions on finalization of the Revised Estimates for 2018-19.
The Department has now put in place a web-based portal for receipt, screening, evaluation and
approval of proposals under all the five schemes, including monitoring of physical and financial
progress of  the  projects to ensure proper utilization of allocated funds under the schemes and
for better financial management.
Further Recommendation
3.11 The Committee would like to be apprised of the projected demands of DHR at stage
2018-19 and the actual allocation made against each scheme. The Committee further  believes
that web-based portal for better monitoring mechanism would yield in efficient  and effective
execution of undertaken schemes/projects.
III INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH (ICMR)
Recommendation
3.12 The Committee observes that in view of the dynamic international health research environment
and the current and future health challenges, the role of ICMR is very crucial. If the projects/
schemes of ICMR are not allocated sufficient funds, it can have serious repercussions and undermine
the desired outcomes in the health sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that more funds
be allocated to ICMR at RE stage well in time so that it can be used judiciously. (Para 3.5)
Action Taken
3.13 The Department appreciates the recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee. The need for
allocation of additional funds would be emphasized with requisite justification at the time of pre-
budgetary discussions in the Ministry of Finance for finalization of RE 2018-19 and BE 2019-20.
Further Recommendation
3.14 The Committee appreciates that ICMR  has been entrusted  with the pivotal task of
formulating conducting and promoting biomedical research with cherished objective of National
Health priorities covering control and management of communicable diseases, fertility control,
maternal and child health, control of nutrational disorders, challenges of environmental and
occupational health problems, conducting  research on non-communicable diseases as well.
The Committee, therefore, desires that the DHR apprise the Committee about the projected
demand of DHR at RE Stage and the actual allocation of fund at RE 2018-19.  The Committee
further believes that DHR would hold effective brain storming  session to assess the actual
requirement of fund for various ongoing/pending and new schemes to be launched  during
2019-20 and accordingly project its demand in BE 2019-20 with due diligence and proper
justification. The Committee would urge Ministry of Finance to consider provision of adequate
fund as component of its fundamental priorities.
Recommendation
3.15 The Committee is concerned about less allocation of funds to ICMR against projected
allocation. The Committee would like to emphasize that ICMR being the only custodian of health
research activities needs to be promoted and encouraged so that tangible outcomes are witnessed

8
for various health care challenges/diseases. The Committee, therefore, lends its support to the
Department’s demand for additional funds to the tune of ` 350.00 crore for 2018-19 at RE stage
and would like to urge upon the Ministry of Finance to increase the budgetary allocation to the
Department  of Health Research so that the Department is able to ensure continuity in critical
health research. (Para 3.8)
Action Taken
3.16 The Department appreciates recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee. The need for allocation
of additional funds would be emphasized with requisite justification at the time of pre-budgetary
discussions in the Ministry of Finance for finalization of RE 2018-19 and BE 2019-20.
Further Recommendation
3.17 The Committee desires the DHR to apprise it whether the Ministry of Finance has
allocated the Department  and additional funds to the tune of `````350.00 crore for 2018-19 at
RE Stage for execution of ongoing schemes as undertaken by ICMR, and ensure that all
research activities are implemented as per set time frames. The Committee also strongly
recommends that Ministry of Finance may consider to allocate adequate fund to ICMR in
the financial year  2019-20 so that research activities of  ICMR do not suffer for want of
fund as outcome of health related research activities would save millions of lives in the
country.
Recommendation
3.18 The Committee observes that allocation of funds for witnessed, an increase of only 
` 3.00 crore
more from the previous ICMR year of RE 2017-18 Given the excellent track-record of  ICMR in
utilizing the budgeted funds, the Committee wonders as to what financial yardstick was applied for
allocation of funds in BE 2018-19 vis-a-vis the projected demand. The Committee, therefore, recommends

to deploy its financial resources in a more efficient manner . (Para 3.9)

3.19 The additional allocation of `247.39 crores made by the Ministry of Finance  in RE 2017-18,

submitted that “against the projected  demand of ````` 2487.00 crore for the year 2018-19 an

On being enquired about the shortfall,  the Department has clarified that atleast ````` 350.00
crore is required to cater ongoing research activities. Out of this ````` 200.00 crore is required
for  ongoing activities and programs (India TB Research Consortium, Malaria Elimination,
INDIAB study, Hypertension study, Human Resource Development and capacity building

programs, Infrastructure Development projects) and ````` 150.00 core for proposed /future
activities and programs (projects related to National Nutrition  Mission, ICMR Academy,
Indo-Africa Initiative, Big Data Analytics, large scale surveys. Mission Mode Projects and

3.21 The Committee, in this connection, recommends  that DHR may persuade the Ministry
of Finance to allocate the fund in Financial year 2019-20 as per actual requirement for
research ongoing/new activities during 2019-20.
Recommendation
3.22 The Committee is also of the view that the ICMR is the main technical wing of the Department
of Health Research and is responsible for formulation, coordination and promotion of bio-medical
research in the country. The Committee,  therefore, notes with serious concern the likely adverse

allocation of additional funds would be emphasized with requisite justification at the time pre-

constraints while implementing its schemes on the intramural and extramural research
activities. The Committee underscore the important impact of projects of ICMR on Bio-
medical research and  developing new drugs, vaccine and diagnostics Kitts in salvaging the
suffering  huge number of mankind from scourge of diseases. The Committee, therefore

that gripped the nation in 2010 and during the Swine flu outbreaks in the past. The Committee,
however, finds that a budget line created in 2015-16 is being allocated meagre amount of 
` 5.00
crore in RE 2017-18 to meet expenditure for supply of diagnostic kits, transport of samples, hiring

II. BUDGET ALLOCATION
Recommendation
1.1  The Committee is constrained to note that despite the projected requirement of 
` 2797.96 crore for
2018-19, the Ministry of AYUSH has been allocated ` 1626.37 crore leaving a shortfall of ` 1171.59 crores.
The Committee also takes note of the meager increase in allocation for central sector and centrally sponsored
schemes from 2017-18 to 2018-19. The Committee, time and again, has been recommending for increasing
the budgetary allocation for the Ministry keeping in view the scope and reach of AYUSH in the life of the
people. Given the popularity, cost effectiveness and as an alternative to modern system of medicine i.e.
Allopathy, the Ministry of AYUSH through its various schemes/ programmes/ vision can help people through
its various remedies/ cure and emerge as a solid system of medicine in healthcare delivery. Accordingly, the
Committee is of the considered view that there needs to be a quantum jump in the budgetary allocation of the
Ministry of AYUSH so that the very objectives of the Ministry to position AYUSH systems as the preferred
system of living and practice for attaining a healthy India is realized. However, in view of the shortfall of
funds for 2018-19, the Committee recommends to the Ministry to judiciously utilize the allocated funds and
deploy the available resources in an efficient manner. (Para 2.4)
Action Taken
1.2 The Ministry agrees with the view of the Committee that there is a need for a quantum jump in the
budgetary allocations so that it can contribute more effectively for attaining a healthy India. To this end, the
Ministry will make every effort to obtain additional funds at RE stage. Further, the recommendation of the
Committee to judiciously utilize the available resources has been taken note and steps will be taken to
regularly monitor the pace of utilization of funds so that remedial action can be taken, if required.
Recommendation
1.3 The Committee is anguished to see the meager allocation given to Ministry of AYUSH compared to
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Since the year 2013-14, allocation for the Ministry of AYUSH is
between 3% to 4% of the Health Budget. It is 3.08% of the Health Budget for the year 2018-19. The
Committee would like to emphasize that the Department of AYUSH was granted the status of Ministry on
9th November, 2014 as it envisaged development and implementation of programmes and policy formulation
for the growth, development and propagation of AYUSH systems of Healthcare. In view of the fact that
the Ministry is being given a miniscule budgetary allocation compared to Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare, the Committee believes that the Ministry of AYUSH would not be able to realize its objectives
and tap the full potential of the AYUSH systems. The Committee would like to reiterate that adequate
funding is essential for proper development of the AYUSH systems of medicine which has the capacity to
emerge as an alternative system of medicine through quality research, quality AYUSH services,
standardization of AYUSH drugs etc. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that given the vital
importance of the AYUSH systems, atleast 5% of the total Health Budget should be allocated for Ministry
of AYUSH mandatorily to boost up this sector. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of
AYUSH should chalk out a solid fiscal roadmap for optimal utilisation of budgeted funds and thereafter
2

3
take up with the Ministry of Finance the issue of earmarking atleast 5% of the total Health Budget for
Ministry of AYUSH on priority basis. In the same vein, the Committee would recommend that the Ministry
should exercise due diligence in its budget formulation, so that ambitious budgeting is commensurate with
its ability or capacity to absorb the enhanced funds and scarce resources deployable elsewhere do not
remain idly parked. (Para 2.6)
Action Taken
1.4 The Ministry proposes to convey to the Ministry of Finance the strong reservations of the Committee
over the inadequate allocation of funds for AYUSH and in particular to raise the allocation to at least 5 per
cent of the total Health Budget towards Ministry of AYUSH on priority basis.  As advised by the Committee,
the Ministry will exercise due diligence in budget formulation and for its optimal deployment.
III. QUALITY  CONTROL  OF  AYURVEDA,  SIDDHA,  UNANI  AND  HOMOEOPATHIC  (AYUSH)
DRUGS
Recommendation
1.5 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry of AYUSH for monitoring of AYUSH
advertisements. Due to the monitoring by Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) and the Grievances
against Misleading Advertisements (GAMA), 65% of the advertisements found misleading were withdrawn
or rectified and the rest forwarded to State AYUSH Drug Regulators. The Committee is of the view that
collaborative efforts of the Ministry along with Department of Consumer Affairs, Ministry of Information
& Broadcasting and State Governments have certainly given results as misleading advertisements with
respect to ASU&H drugs which have been unregulated so far have been controlled to an extent. The Committee
feels that it is the need of the hour to strictly monitor and regulate the misleading advertisements for
promoting the sale of AYUSH medicine. Hence, the role of the Ministry of AYUSH is pivotal in proactively
pursuing the issue with other Departments/ Ministries/ ASCI on a regular basis for effectively preventing the
publication of inappropriate/misleading advertisements. (Para 3.12)
Action Taken
1.6 Ministry has proactively pursued the matter of controlling the misleading advertisements of AYUSH
with the following steps-
(i) The matter of misleading AYUSH advertisements appearing in print and electronic media has
been taken up with the media regulators like Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology
and Ministry of Information & Broadcasting and their suggestions/comments incorporated in
evolving the provisions of rules for prohibition of such advertisements.  The draft rules thus
framed have been subjected to consultation with the Drugs Controller General (India) and
Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani Drugs Technical Advisory Board (ASUDTAB) for concurrence and
to enable further action.
(ii) Ministry of Information & Broadcasting issued instructions/guidelines dated 12th July, 2017 to
all media channels to advertise only those AYUSH products which have valid manufacturing
license and to abstain from telecasting such misleading advertisements which are in contravention
of the provisions of the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
and Rules thereunder.

4
(iii) Ne wly implemented Central Scheme of Pharmacovigilance of ASU&H Drugs also has a
component of monitoring of misleading advertisement by the peripheral centres of the
pharmacovigilance network being developed.
(iv) An Empowered Committee of interdepartmental officers has recently been notified with specific
ToRs of periodic review, monitoring and recommendations for necessary remedial measures
to address the issues and complaints of exaggerated claims and inappropriate advertisements
of AYUSH.
(v) Ministry conducted seven regulatory & quality control training programs of AYUSH across the
country from 22 January, 2018 to 17
thMarch, 2018 for the regulators & manufacturers, in
which intense focus was imparted to the trainees/participants about the technical and regulatory
irregularities of AYUSH advertisements and the provisions of Drugs & Magic Remedies
(Objectionable Advertisements) Act and Rules.
(vi) S tates/UTs have been directed to appoint Gazetted Officers for territorial monitoring of AYUSH
advertisements under the provisions of  Drugs & Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements)
Act and to nominate Nodal Officers for dealing with public complaints of misleading AYUSH
advertisements registered in the GAMA (Grievances Against Misleading Advertisements) Portal
maintained by the Department of Consumer Affairs.
(vii) During the period from 20th January, 2017 to 19th January, 2018, about 456 complaints of
misleading AYUSH advertisements are reported to have been escalated to the State regulators

Recommendation
2.1 The Committee has been given to understand that the funds remained unutilised for some schemes
of the Ministry due to non-receipt of suitable project proposals, delay in the construction work and
transfer of money to various institutes for starting extension centres. The Committee perceives the reasons
for under-utilization of funds as procedural hickups which could have been avoided if the Ministry had
proactively pursued the issues concerned and streamlined its monitoring mechanism. The Committee takes
cognizance of the steps taken by the Ministry for optimum utilization of funds but would like to emphasize
that if the Ministry needs more budgetary allocation for proper implementation of its various schemes/
programmes, it should be able to show judicious and full utilization of allocated funds thereby justifying
its demand for additional funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to closely monitor
the utilization of funds for any  scheme and take corrective measures so as to expedite matters where

III. QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDA, SIDDHA, UNANI AND HOMOEOPATHIC (AYUSH)
DRUGS
Recommendation
3.4 The Committee is of the view that a strong and strict regulatory framework is essential for quality
control of ASU&H drugs. Since the States are responsible for quality control and regulation of AYUSH
drugs, they need financial assistance so as to strengthen their regulatory framework. The Committee notes
that the financial assistance given to States is not much and therefore reiterates its recommendation as given
in 101
st Report for significant enhancement of financial assistance to the States. (Para 3.6)
Action Taken
3.5  The funding pattern to support regulatory and quality control activities of AYUSH drugs in the states
has been enhanced significantly in the National AYUSH Mission (NAM) implemented since November,
2014. In comparison to the erstwhile Central Sponsored Scheme, the funding pattern under the National
AYUSH Mission has been enhanced up to ` 5 crores for state pharmacy, up to ` 4 crores for Drug Testing
Laboratory (DTL), up to ` 50 lakhs for strengthening of regulatory framework, up to ` 25 lakhs per year
for technical manpower of the DTL and up to ` 15 lakhs per year for testing of drug samples.  Nevertheless,
it is for the states to project their requirement of financial assistance in the State Annual Action Plan (SAAP)
of National AYUSH Mission inter-alia for the purpose of quality control of ASU&H drugs and accordingly
the funds are released after necessary approval.
Further Recommendation
3.6 India has a rich heritage of AYUSH systems of medicine, which are widely recognized for
their holistic approach to healthcare.  However, one of the greatest challenges to widespread acceptance
of AYUSH drugs remains quality assurance. Strengthening and modernization of regulatory
framework for quality control of ASU&H drugs is, therefore, a pre-requisite for a strong and effective
system of AYUSH remedies for which it is necessary to step up allocation to State AYUSH drug
regulatory mechanisms.  Though the Committee appreciates the fact that the funding pattern to
support regulatory and quality control activities of the AYUSH drugs in the States has witnessed
improvements since the implementation of National AYUSH Mission in November, 2014, it feels
that a lot more remains to be done to bridge the regulatory gaps.  The Committee would therefore
like the Ministry to sensitize the States to the fact that for equipping AYUSH to achieve tangible
health outcomes, it is imperative that the weakness in the regulatory framework are addressed and
a significant proportion of outlay is projected in their Annual Action Plan for supporting quality
assurance activities.  The Committee desires to be apprised of the initiatives taken by the Ministry
in this regard.
Recommendation
3.7 The Committee would also like to express concern about the issue of failed samples of ASU drugs and
the consequent action taken in this regard. The Committee is of the firm view that merely issuing show cause
notices, departmental action etc. is not enough to control the menace of spurious drugs of AYUSH. Despite
repeated recommendations of the Committee to have stringent measures to tackle the problem of failed
samples, the Ministry seems not to have done anything in this regard. The Committee takes serious note of
the lackadaisical approach of the Ministry in not taking concrete action against defaulters in order to ensure

14
effective regulation of ASU&H drugs. The Committee would like to emphasize that such erring manufacturers
need to be brought to book and dealt with strictly for misleading and duping innocent patients and playing
with their lives. The Committee, accordingly, recommends to the Ministry to lay down stringent regulations
which can act as a deterrent for erring manufacturers. (Para 3.7)
Action Taken
3.8 Misbranded, Adulterated, Spurious and Sub-standard ASU drugs are defined in the Drugs & Cosmetics
Act, 1940 along with the provisions for prohibition of their manufacturing, sale, stocking and distribution;
and the penalty in the form of confiscation of the concerned batch of the drug and payment of fine and/or
imprisonment of the defaulters. As per statute, the power of enforcing these provisions is vested with the
state governments. The states have reported confiscation of such cases of ASU drugs; suspension/ cancellation
of the manufacturing licenses; and prosecution of the defaulters. The Central Government has in the past
banned/ prohibited the manufacturing and sale of ASU products made from tobacco, certain alcoholic
preparations, injections, etc. In order to enforce the ASU drugs related legal provisions in the effective
manner, following steps have been taken:
(i) Ministry of AYUSH has written to the States and supported them for testing of adequate
number of AYUSH drug samples and initiate legal action against the defaulters;
(ii) During 2017-18, the Ministry conducted seven regulatory and quality control training programs
for the ASU&H drug regulators, pharmacy and laboratory staff including manufacturers of all
the states/ UTs;
(iii) An A YUSH vertical has been created in the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization
(CDSCO) w.e.f. 5
th February, 2018 with 12 regulatory posts of Inspectors, Assistant Drugs
Controllers and Deputy Drugs Controllers at the Central level;
(iv) Central sector scheme for safety monitoring of AYUSH drugs and surveillance of the misleading
advertisements has been implemented in 2017-18 to develop an institutional network for detection,
assessment, documenting and reporting of the Adverse Drug Reactions of AYUSH drugs for
appropriate regulatory action;
(v) Financial assistance is being provided through National AYUSH Mission for strengthening the
regulatory and quality control system in the states.
Further Recommendation
3.9 The Committee understands that the power of enforcing the provisions of the Drugs &
Cosmetics Act, 1940 is vested with the State Government.  However, the Central Government is
involved through its schemes and initiatives wherein financial assistance for strengthening the
quality control system through NAM, Central Sector Scheme for safety monitoring of AYUSH
drugs, quality control training programmes in States, creation of a vertical structure in CDSCO
etc is given.  The Committee is of the view that the actual work of the newly created vertical
structure in CDSCO in quality control of drugs and work done for safety monitoring of AYUSH
drugs under the Central Sector Scheme are yet to be seen.  Apart from that, as earlier observed
by the Committee itself, merely issuing directions, show cause notices etc is not sufficient to deal
with the alarming issue at hand.  The Committee has been impressing upon the Ministry to carry
out the required amendment to Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 so that stringent clauses are included

15
in the Act to effectively deter the erring manufacturers. The Committee however, regrets to
observe that no headway has been made in this regard and desires to be apprised of the hindrances
in this regard. The Committee is aware that the power of enforcing quality control provisions
falls within the purview of State Governments. Nonetheless, given the fact that a part of the plan
outlay of the Ministry is allocated for quality assurance activities, the Committee expects the
Ministry to play a more dynamic role and it is therefore, imperative that certain festering issues
afflicting quality assurance of AYUSH drugs are taken up by the Ministry and corrective measures
suggested thereon.
Recommendation
3.10 Attention of the Committee has been drawn to the fact that last year, 29 Drug laboratories and 46
Pharmacies were available in the public sector in the States and 6 States did not have any manufacturing
unit. The Committee in its 101
st report 2017-18 had recommended that there should be atleast one Drug
Testing Laboratory in each State and more ASU&H drug manufacturing units in the country. The Ministry
in its submission has not given any information about the increase in States Drug Testing Laboratories,
Pharmacies and ASU&H drug manufacturing units. The Committee is constrained to note that the progress
of GMP compliance by manufacturing units across the country has also not been furnished by the Ministry.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Ministry should strive for increasing the number of State
Drug Testing Laboratories for effective regulation of ASU&H drugs and manufacturing units which should
be GMP compliant for producing quality drugs for the people. The Ministry should also furnish the relevant
information to the Committee properly. (Para 3.9)
Action Taken
3.11 During the year 2017-18, seven pharmacies and nine Drug Testing Laboratories in the states have
been provided grant-in-aid through National AYUSH Mission (NAM). In this regard, attention of the Hon’ble
Committee is kindly drawn to the fact that it is the prerogative of State/UT Governments to submit the
proposals for seeking grant-in-aid for establishment or strengthening of pharmacies and laboratories in their
State Annual Action Plans under National AYUSH Mission.
3.12 Besides the availability of Central and State Drug Testing Laboratories, 55 private laboratories are
approved or licensed as of now under the provisions of Drugs& Cosmetic Rules, 1945 and proposals of
more such laboratories are in the pipeline for grant of approval.
3.13 Schedule ‘T’ and Schedule ‘M-I’ under Drugs & Cosmetics Rules, 1945 contain the provisions
of Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) for ASU and Homoeopathic drugs respectively. GMP for the
manufacturing of ASU drugs was introduced w.e.f. 7.3.2003 and for Homoeopathic drugs w.e.f.
31.10.2006. As per the available information, 8667 licensed manufacturing units of ASU&H drugs exist
in the country, out of which 7488 (86.7%) units are GMP compliant and 1179 (13.6%) units are
reported not to be complying with GMP norms. Detailed information of State-wise progress about the
number of pharmacies,  GMP compliant units and laboratories for ASU&H drugs from 2015 to current
position is annexed as Annexure-I .
Further Recommendation
3.14 The Committee has been given to understand that there are 88 drug testing laboratories
in the country. The States of Goa, Manipur  and the UTs of Andaman and Nicobar, Dadar &

16
Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu, Lakshadweep & Puduchery are not having any labs. There were a
total of 9282 Pharmacies in the 36 States/ UTs of the country as on 1 st April, 2015, out of which
7653 were GMP compliant. Presently, there are 8667 Pharmacies, out of which 7488 only are
GMP compliant. The Committee notes that the number of pharmacies has reduced from 9282 to
8667 with maximum reduction in the State of Tamil Nadu.  Apart from that, the number of GMP
compliant units has also declined from 7653 to 7488. The Committee wonders about such decrease
in numbers and the reasons for such a trend is not clear.  The Committee is constrained to note
such decrease in the total number of pharmacies in 2018 compared to 2015. The Committee,
accordingly, would like the Ministry to have an assessment done so as to ascertain the reasons
for the same in consultation with the State Governments especially Tamil Nadu. The Committee
would also like to emphasize that the Ministry needs to make concerted efforts in co-ordination
with State Governments to make these units GMP complaint. Further, States/ UTs where there
are no labs as of now need to be engaged and prompted to contemplate about having atleast one
lab in the State/ UTs.
Recommendation
3.15 With respect to the new legislation containing the existing and proposed provisions of both Drugs and
Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisement) Act, 1954, the Committee
is dismayed to note that the new legislation is still in the process of being framed by the Department of
Health and Family Welfare. It has been more than two years since the new legislation is being framed and
it speaks volumes about the laid back approach of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and also of
the Ministry of AYUSH in pursuing the matter. The Committee would like to strongly recommend that a
definite time line within which this new legislation will see the light of the day may be indicated and the
Ministry of AYUSH should aggressively pursue the matter with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare so
that relevant provisions are incorporated in the legislation and enacted so as to prohibit misleading
advertisements and strengthen the effective regulation of ASU&H drugs. (Para 3.13)
Action Taken
3.16 Drugs & Cosmetics Act,1940 is under the administrative purview of Ministry of Health & Family
Welfare. Accordingly, on the recommendations of the Group of Ministers, the Department of Health &
Family Welfare did take up the task of framing new legislation for Drugs & Cosmetics including Ayurvedic,
Siddha, Unni, Sowa Rigpa and Homoeopathic drugs. For this purpose, Ministry of AYUSH provided
necessary inputs for framing ASU& H drugs related regulatory provisions including stringent penal provisions
for violation of quality norms and standards. The proposed provisions were conceptualized in accordance
with the emerging regulatory trends for effective quality control of ASU&H drugs. The Ministry is pursuing
the matter of imposing effective quality control of ASU&H drugs and introducing prohibitive measures
for misleading advertisements and has inter alia constituted two Empowered Committees chaired by Joint
Secretary level officers vide office order dated 22.3.2018 to monitor the progress of new regulatory
vertical structure of AYUSH in CDSCO and control of misleading advertisement/exaggerated claims
respectively.
Further Recommendation
3.17 The Committee is relieved to know that the Ministry has provided necessary inputs for framing
ASU&H drugs related regulatory provisions for framing a new legislation regarding violation of

17
quality norms and standards.  The Committee, however, is of the view that given the seriousness of
the situation in wake of sale of spurious/ sub-standard ASU drugs, the matter of bringing in a new
legislation in this regard needs to be taken up with the Department of Health and Family Welfare
on a priority basis.  The Committee would also like to be apprised of the composition of the two
Empowered Committees constituted in March, 2018 and the work done by the two Committees with
respect to the regulatory vertical structure of AYUSH for quality assurance and control of misleading
advertisement/ exaggerated claims.
IV. NATIONAL  AYUSH  MISSION
Recommendation
3.18 The Committee appreciates the Ministry of AYUSH for having co-location of AYUSH facilities
at PHCs, CHCs and District Hospitals, participation of AYUSH doctors in National Health Programme
and Public Health Outreach Activities and research activities undertaken to facilitate integration of
Ayurveda and Allopathic system of medicine. The Committee would, however, like to point out that
it is often seen that practitioners of modern system of medicine do not have much faith in AYUSH
system and often question their credibility and scientific validation. The Committee feels that it is a
known fact that our country has been a repository of knowledge of traditional systems of medicine
since ages. The need of the hour is to streamline the AYUSH systems of medicine by standardisation
and quality control of ASU&H drugs and improving the quality of education and healthcare services
through AYUSH. At the same time, the curricula of both modern systems of medicine and AYUSH
system need to be changed in such a way as to strive for integration in the study of medical education
itself followed by cross system referrals and integrated healthcare services. The Committee is of the
view that such an integrated approach towards both systems of medicine would help in understanding
the strengths of each system of medicine and also increase the credibility of AYUSH systems of
medicine. The Committee, accordingly, recommends to the Ministry to take concrete steps in introducing
modules of modern system of medicine in the curriculum and pursue the Ministry of Health and
Family Welfare for introducing similar modules of AYUSH systems of medicines in their MBBS
course. (Para 4.10)
Action Taken
3.19 It may be stated here that the National Policy on Indian Systems of Medicine & Homoeopathy –
2002, envisages integration of AYUSH with the Health Care Delivery System.  Mainstreaming of AYUSH
is one of the strategies in National Health Mission (NHM) as well which seeks to provide accessible,
affordable and quality health care in order to improve the existing health care delivery system.  Government
of India has adopted a strategy of Co-location of AYUSH facilities at Primary Health Centres (PHCs),
Community Health Centres (CHCs) and District Hospitals (DHs), thus enabling choice to the patients for
different systems of medicines under single window.  The engagement of AYUSH Doctors/ paramedics
and their training is supported by the Department of Health & Family Welfare, while the support for
AYUSH infrastructure, equipment/ furniture and medicines are provided by Ministry of AYUSH under
shared responsibilities.
So far as curricula or integrated course and Bridge course is concerned, no such initiatives has been
taken by the Ministry presently.

18
Further Recommendation
3.20 The Committee appreciates the strategy of the National Policy on Indian Systems of Medicine
and Homoeopathy 2002 which envisages integration of AYUSH with health care delivery system
leading to co-location of AYUSH facilities at PHCs, CHCs and District Hospitals. The Committee in
order to bring AYUSH into the mainstream had recommended for change in curriculum which
would include introducing modules of modern medicine in AYUSH system and modules of AYUSH in
the curriculum of modern medicine i.e. MBBS course.  The Committee is of the firm view that the
Ministry of AYUSH needs to take initiative in promoting and integrating Indian systems of medicine
with the modern systems so as to increase its acceptability as a scientific and reliable alternate
system of medicine. The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that the Ministry must lay
focus on increasing the credibility of AYUSH systems by promoting scientific research and upholding
strict quality control of AYUSH drugs.  The Committee, therefore, would like to recommend to the
Ministry to engage with Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for integration of AYUSH systems
with modern medicine.
Recommendation
3.21 The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of AYUSH should earmark a substantial amount of
funds for collaborative research with ICMR for the purposes of standardization and scientific re-validation
of ASU&H drugs. In this way, ASU&H drugs/ remedies will have worldwide acceptance and scientific basis
of AYUSH will be augmented. (Para 5.8)

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS  —  AT A GLANCE
II. BUDGET ALLOCATION
The Committee is disappointed to note that although the Ministry is making efforts for
liquidation of pending UCs, the issue of high pendency of UCs is not solved.  The Committee is also
unhappy to note that the Ministry has not apprised the Committee about the operationalization of
the digital portal which may actually help in speedy transmission and liquidation of UCs.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the digital online portal needs to be operationalised at the
earliest so that the matter of pendency of UCs is solved.  The Committee also would like the
Ministry to lay special focus on the two schemes, namely, National Medicinal Plants Board and
National AYUSH Mission where number of pendency of UCs is quite high. (Para 3.3)
III. QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDA, SIDDHA, UNANI AND HOMOEOPATHIC (AYUSH)
DRUGS
India has a rich heritage of AYUSH systems of medicine, which are widely recognized for
their holistic approach to healthcare.  However, one of the greatest challenges to widespread acceptance
of AYUSH drugs remains quality assurance. Strengthening and modernization of regulatory
framework for quality control of ASU&H drugs is, therefore, a pre-requisite for a strong and effective
system of AYUSH remedies for which it is necessary to step up allocation to State AYUSH drug
regulatory mechanisms.  Though the Committee appreciates the fact that the funding pattern to
support regulatory and quality control activities of the AYUSH drugs in the States has witnessed
improvements since the implementation of National AYUSH Mission in November, 2014, it feels
that a lot more remains to be done to bridge the regulatory gaps.  The Committee would therefore
like the Ministry to sensitize the States to the fact that for equipping AYUSH to achieve tangible
health outcomes, it is imperative that the weakness in the regulatory framework are addressed and
a significant proportion of outlay is projected in their Annual Action Plan for supporting quality
assurance activities.  The Committee desires to be apprised of the initiatives taken by the Ministry
in this regard. (Para 3.6)
The Committee understands that the power of enforcing the provisions of the Drugs &
Cosmetics Act, 1940 is vested with the State Government.  However, the Central Government is
involved through its schemes and initiatives wherein financial assistance for strengthening the
quality control system through NAM, Central Sector Scheme for safety monitoring of AYUSH
drugs, quality control training programmes in States, creation of a vertical structure in CDSCO
etc is given.  The Committee is of the view that the actual work of the newly created vertical
structure in CDSCO in quality control of drugs and work done for safety monitoring of AYUSH
drugs under the Central Sector Scheme are yet to be seen.  Apart from that, as earlier observed
by the Committee itself, merely issuing directions, show cause notices etc is not sufficient to deal
with the alarming issue at hand.  The Committee has been impressing upon the Ministry to carry
out the required amendment to Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 so that stringent clauses are included
in the Act to effectively deter the erring manufacturers. The Committee however, regrets to
observe that no headway has been made in this regard and desires to be apprised of the hindrances
in this regard. The Committee is aware that the power of enforcing quality control provisions
falls within the purview of State Governments. Nonetheless, given the fact that a part of the plan
outlay of the Ministry is allocated for quality assurance activities, the Committee expects the
22

23
Ministry to play a more dynamic role and it is therefore, imperative that certain festering issues
afflicting quality assurance of AYUSH drugs are taken up by the Ministry and corrective measures
suggested thereon. (Para 3.9)
The Committee has been given to understand that there are 88 drug testing laboratories
in the country. The States of Goa, Manip ur and the UTs of Andaman and Nicobar, Dadar &
Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu, Lakshadweep & Puduchery are not having any labs. There were a
total of 9282 Pharmacies in the 36 States/ UTs of the country as on 1
st April, 2015, out of which
7653 were GMP compliant. Presently, there are 8667 Pharmacies, out of which 7488 only are
GMP compliant. The Committee notes that the number of pharmacies has reduced from 9282 to
8667 with maximum reduction in the State of Tamil Nadu.  Apart from that, the number of GMP
compliant units has also declined from 7653 to 7488. The Committee wonders about such decrease
in numbers and the reasons for such a trend is not clear.  The Committee is constrained to note
such decrease in the total number of pharmacies in 2018 compared to 2015. The Committee,
accordingly, would like the Ministry to have an assessment done so as to ascertain the reasons
for the same in consultation with the State Governments especially Tamil Nadu. The Committee
would also like to emphasize that the Ministry needs to make concerted efforts in co-ordination
with State Governments to make these units GMP complaint. Further, States/ UTs where there
are no labs as of now need to be engaged and prompted to contemplate about having atleast one
lab in the State/ UTs. (Para 3.14)
The Committee is relieved to know that the Ministry has provided necessary inputs for framing
ASU&H drugs related regulatory provisions for framing a new legislation regarding violation of
quality norms and standards.  The Committee, however , is of the view that given the seriousness of
the situation in wake of sale of spurious/ sub-standard ASU drugs, the matter of bringing in a new
legislation in this regard needs to be taken up with the Department of Health and Family Welfare
on a priority basis.  The Committee would also like to be apprised of the composition of the two
Empowered Committees constituted in March, 2018 and the work done by the two Committees with
respect to the regulatory vertical structure of AYUSH for quality assurance and control of misleading
advertisement/ exaggerated claims. (Para 3.17)
IV. NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION
The Committee appreciates the strategy of the National Policy on Indian Systems of Medicine
and Homoeopathy 2002 which envisages integration of AYUSH with health care delivery system
leading to co-location of AYUSH facilities at PHCs, CHCs and District Hospitals. The Committee in
order to bring AYUSH into the mainstream had recommended for change in curriculum which
would include introducing modules of modern medicine in AYUSH system and modules of AYUSH in
the curriculum of modern medicine i.e. MBBS course.  The Committee is of the firm view that the
Ministry of AYUSH needs to take initiative in promoting and integrating Indian systems of medicine
with the modern systems so as to increase its acceptability as a scientific and reliable alternate
system of medicine. The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that the Ministry must lay
focus on increasing the credibility of AYUSH systems by promoting scientific research and upholding
strict quality control of AYUSH drugs.  The Committee, therefore, would like to recommend to the
Ministry to engage with Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for integration of AYUSH systems
with modern medicine. (Para 3.20)

specifically, the funds allocated to these research institutes were not sufficient and needed to be

again like to emphasize that in order to increase the popularity and acceptability of Indian Systems

so as to increase the credibility of AYUSH systems by promoting standardization, scientific re-

REPORT 
CHAPTER - I 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1 Mission Statement of the Bill 
1.1.1 According to the Statement of Objects and Reasons, the National Commission for Indian 
System of Medicine Bill, 2019 seeks to provide for constitution of a National Commission for 
Indian System of Medicine for development and regulation of all aspects relat ing to education, 
medical profession and medical institutions of Indian System of Medicine and an Advisory 
Council to advise and make recommendations to the Commission to achieve the mission 
objectives of the Bill as enshrined in its Preamble.  
1.1.2 The P reamble to the Bill aims to provide a medical education system that improves 
access to quality and affordable medical education and to ensure availability of adequate and 
high quality medical professionals of Indian System of Medicine in all parts of the c ountry.  The 
Bill also seeks to promote equitable and universal healthcare that encourages community health 
perspective and makes services of such medical professionals accessible to all the citizens. In 
order to achieve the national health goals, the Bill  encourages such medical professionals to 
adopt latest medical research in their work and to contribute to research.  It envisages a system 
that has an objective, periodic and transparent assessment of medical institutions. The Bill 
facilitates maintenance of a medical register of Indian System of Medicine for India and enforces 
high ethical standards in all aspects of medical services. 
1.1.3 Broadly speaking, the Bill is a replica of National Medical Commission Bill, 2019  (Now 
an Act ( No. 30 of  2019) the G azette of India, Part II, Section -1, 8 th August, 2019) . It entails 
constitution of Autonomous Boards, holding of NEET, NEXT, National Entrance Test and 
National Teachers Eligibility Test and strives to adapt to the changing needs and keep pace with 
the time and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. 
1.2 Objectives of the Bill  
1.2.1 The National Commission for Indian System of Medicine, Bill 2019, inter alia, seeks to 
provide for—  
(a) constitution of a National Commission for Indian System of Medicine for development and 
regulation of all aspects relating to education, medical profession and medical institutions of 
Indian System of Medicine and an Advisory Council to advise and make recommendations 
to the Commission; 
(b)  constitution of four Autonomous Boards, namely:  
(i) the Board of Ayurveda to regulate Ayurveda education at undergraduate and 
postgraduate levels and to determine standards thereof;  

2 
 
(ii) the Board of Unani, Siddha and Sowa -Rigpa to regulate education at undergraduate 
and postgraduate levels and to determine standards thereof; 
(iii) the Medical Assessment and Rating Board for Indian System of Medicine to carry 
out inspections and to assess and rate the medical institutions; and 
(iv) the Board of Ethics and  Registration for Indian System of Medicine to regulate 
professional conduct and promote medical ethics amongst practitioners and professionals 
of Indian Medicine and to maintain a national register of all licensed practitioners of 
Indian Medicine; 
(c) holding of a uniform National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for admission to undergraduate 
medical education; 
(d) holding of a National Exit Test for granting licence to practice as medical practitioner of 
Indian System of Medicine; 
(e) holding of a uniform Post-Graduate National Entrance Test for postgraduate courses; 
(f) holding of National Teachers' Eligibility Test for Indian System of Medicine for appointment 
as teachers thereto; 
(g) the manner of seeking permission for establishment of new medical institution; 
(h) the manner of maintaining National Register and State Register of Indian System of 
Medicine; 
(i)  recognition of medical qualification granted by Universities and medical institutions in India 
and outside India and withdrawal of recognition or de-recognition of qualification; 
(j) holding of joint sitting of the Commissions of other medical education to enhance interface 
between Indian System of Medicine, Homoeopathy and modern system of medicine; 
(k) the repeal of the Indian Medicine Central Council, Act, 1970 and for dissolution of the 
Central Council of Indian Medicine constituted thereunder with certain conditions. 
1.3 Background and Necessity of the Bill  
1.3.1 According to Statement of Objects and Reasons (SOR) of the Bill, the Indian Med icine 
Central Council (IMCC) Act, 1970 (48 of 1970) was enacted to provide a solid foundation for 
the growth of medical education of Indian Systems of Medicine, namely, Ayurveda, Unani, 
Siddha and Sowa -Rigpa and to provide for constitution of the Central C ouncil of Indian 
Medicine for regulation of the educational standards of Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, and Sowa -
Rigpa systems of medicine, maintenance of the Central Register of practitioners and for matters 
connected therewith. The said Act has not kept pace w ith time. Various bottlenecks viz. (i) 

3 
 
irregularities in regulation of AYUSH medical institutions, (ii) ineffective role of members and 
Executive Committee, (iii) lack of standard curriculum and education,  (iv) absence of ethics in 
practice of Indian Syste m of Medicine, (v) failure to provide transparent system of inspection 
and (vi) alleged irregularities in grant of recognition & de -recognition of education system have 
crept into the system with serious detrimental effects on medical education and by implication on 
delivery of quality health services. 
1.3.2 The SOR of the Bill further stipulates that in order to streamline the functioning of the 
Central Council of Indian Medicine, to bring transparency in the mechanism for grant of 
permission to medical in stitutions and to improve the standards of medical education in Indian 
Systems of Medicine, the Central Government had introduced the Indian Medicine Central 
Council (Amendment) Bill, 2005 in Rajya Sabha which is still pending. In 2016, the Central 
Government constituted a Committee chaired by Vice -Chairman, NITI Aayog to review the 
Indian Medicine Central Council Act and the said Committee recommended for enactment of the 
National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Bill, 2018 on the same lines as tha t of the 
National Medical Commission Bill, 2018. 
1.3.3 Replying to the Committee’s query about the details of the factors that hindered the 
effective implementation of the provisions of the Central Council of Indian Medicine (CCIM) 
Act, 1970, the Ministry of AYUSH pointed out the following lacunae in the Act:-  
Absence of effective provisions in IMCC Act rel ating to constitution of council, membership to 
have transparent selection of members and their tenure; no provision in the Act for taking action 
against the college for non -compliance of standards, non –conduction of fair inspections and  
recommendation by the Council; no conditions for removal of members from the Council or for 
superseding the Council on account of any untoward incident or act.  
1.3.4 The Committee desired to know the reasons that have led to the failure of Central 
Council of Indian Medicine  (CCIM) in  monitoring the  higher education in Indian systems of 
medicine, including  Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani and the main problems/hindrances/obstac les 
being faced by CCIM in regulating the practice of the Indian Systems of Medicine.   
1.3.5 In reply to this query, t he Ministry submitted that t he Indian Medicine Central Council 
(IMCC) Act, 1970 was enacted for constitution of a Central Council of Indian Medicine (CCIM); 
for regulation of education and practic e of Indian Systems of Medicine;  for maintenance of 
Central Register and for matters connected therewith.  The lack of effective provisions in the Act 
to address the issues relating to Membersh ip, conditions for removal of Members/President in 
case of non-performance or otherwise, lack of power of Central Government to make regulations 
or supersede the Council and lack of penalizing provisions on institutes for non -compliance of 
prescribed standards were some of the lacking provisions in the Act which also led to  members 
continuing beyond 5 years tenure.  
1.3.6 The Ministry further submitted that t he Inspection of colleges being conducted by the 
Council has been observed to be unfair. The Council  had not implemented the suggestions of 
Government like Aadhar based geo -location enabled attendance system for teachers, Hospital 

4 
 
staff and PG students, NEET, and Teachers eligibility test. The Council failed to ensure 
standards in colleges and no steps h ave been taken to improve the teaching and training skills of 
teachers. The Council could not unfold the hidden potentialities of the Indian systems of 
medicine.” 
1.3.7 The 9 th Report of the Planning Commission, Government of India noted that under the 
Indian System of Medicine “training Institutes lack well qualified teachers and the quality of 
training was not of requisite standard.” The National Policy on Indian System of Medicine and 
Homoeopathy, 2002 also mentioned that “Medical education in Indian Sys tem of Medicine and 
Homoeopathy has been a cause of concern . The numbers of Indian System of Medicine and 
Homoeopathy Colleges has increased phenomenally to 404 (729 colleges at present). The 
Central Councils have implemented various educational regulation s to ensure minimum 
standards of education. Despite this, there has been a mushrooming of sub -standard colleges 
causing erosion to the standards of education and harm to medical training and practice. 
Liberal permission by the State Governments, loopholes in the existing Acts and weakness in the 
enforcement of standards of education have contributed to this state of affairs.”   
1.3.8 It was, therefore, felt by the Committee that there is a need to amend some of the 
provisions of the IMCC Act, 1970 and CCIM with respect to establishment of new medical 
colleges, increasing seats and granting permission to existing medical colleges. 
1.3.9 The Government of India took some steps to meet the challenges Central Council of 
Indian Medicine (CCIM) and to resolve these bottlenecks. 
1.4 The Indian Medicine Central Council (Amendment Bill)-2005 
1.4.1 The Central Council of Indian Medicine was initially constituted through nomination of 
members in 1971. Subsequently, elections to the said Council were conducted. Though the 
tenure of all the members of the said Council elected in 1994 -95 had expired in 2000, it could 
not be reconstituted even after a lapse of more than four years because the election process had 
been completed only in 7 States out of 18 States that mainta ined the State Register of Indian 
Medicine. In fact the State Register of Indian Medicine was not updated, at the instance of sitting 
members which is a pre-requisite for conducting elections in time. Sometimes, the elections were 
delayed due to litigation  and stay orders from court. To ensure timely election to the Central 
Council of Indian Medicine and to streamline its functioning, the following provisions  were 
made in the Indian Medicine Central Council (Amendment) Bill  2005.  
(i) To nominate ex-officio members 
(ii) To have fix tenure of elected or nominated members 
(iii) To remove the President, Vice -president and members on grounds of misconduct or 
incapacity; 
(iv) To dissolve any committee of the Central Council if it persistently defaults or abuses 
its powers; and 
(v) To give directions to the Council in the public interest. 

5 
 
1.5 Indian Medicine Central Council (Amendment) Bill, 2010 
1.5.1 Before the IMCC Amendment Bill, 2010, Indian Medicine Central Council comprised of 
members elected from amongst the practitioners of Ayur veda, Siddha and Unani whose names 
were enrolled in the State Registers from Universities having the faculty or Department of 
Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani and members nominated by the Central Government from amongst 
the persons having special knowledge or pr actical experience in respect of Indian Systems of 
Medicine. The “Sowa Rigpa” system of medicine practiced in the Sub –Himalayan region was 
included as a system within the definition of “Indian Medicine” and the practitioners of the Sowa 
Rigpa system were enrolled in the Register so as to develop the system and its practices within a 
legal framework. Sowa Rigpa was given formal recognition as part of ISM in 2010. With time, 
the number of colleges imparting training and education in ISM had been increasing bu t many 
colleges failed on quality and standard parameter. To monitor this rapid proliferation of poor 
quality colleges, the IMCC Act was amended and some provisions were inserted in the Act. 
1.6 The National Commission for Human Resources for Health Bill, 2011 
1.6.1 While considering the observations and recommendations of Parliamentary Standing 
Committee of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the proposal of Department of Health 
for establishing an overarching body namely, “National Commission for H uman Resources in 
Health (NCHRH)” was introduced. Accordingly, the Ministry conceived a similar proposal for 
establishing an overarching body namely National Commission for Human Resources in 
AYUSH (NCHRA), which was modeled on the National Commission for Human Resources in 
Health (NCHRH). The Department of Health and Family Welfare did not pursue the proposed 
Bill. Therefore, the Ministry of AYUSH dropped the idea of setting up of National Commission 
for Human Resources in AYUSH. 
1.7 The Committee under the Chairmanship of Vice Chairman, NITI AAYOG 
1.7.1 In the process of streamlining and reforming the functioning of Central Council of Indian 
Medicine (CCIM) and Central Council of Homeopathy (CCH) and their legislations, the Central 
Government vide its OM No. 4(3)/2016 -H&FW dated 04.08.2016 had set up a Co mmittee under 
the Chairmanship of Vice -Chairman, NITI Aayog, with Additional Principal Secretary to PM, 
CEO, NITI Ayog and Secretary, AYUSH as members. This Committee was tasked to examine 
Homoeopathy Central Council (HCC) Act, 1973 and Indian Medicine Cen tral Council (IMCC) 
Act, 1970 and to suggest necessary reforms for improving education in the Indian Systems of 
Medicine and Homoeopathy in India. 
1.7.2 The Committee sought views and suggestions of various experts including eminent 
Indian Systems of Medic ine and Homoeopathy practitioners; representatives of renowned 
institutes for Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy Education and Research; former 
Secretaries to the Government of India, Department of AYUSH; modern medicine practitioners; 
President/Vice-President and other Members of the CCIM and CCH. Representations were also 
received from common citizens as well as experts.  

6 
 
1.7.3 NITI AYOG  in its Preliminary Report stated that Central Council of Indian Medicine 
CCIM has failed to:- 
(i) Bring in competen t and qualified persons based on merit for regulating AYUSH 
medical education; the nominated members of CCIM (30%) have not succeeded 
in making an effective impact over the elected members.  
(ii) Create standard curricula that can produce quality doctors in Ind ian Systems of 
Medicine. 
(iii) Maintain uniform standards of medical education at the under -graduate and post -
graduate levels.  
(iv) Ensure ethics in the practice of Indian Systems of Medicine. 
(v) Ensure quality enforcement mechanisms.  
(vi) Create a transparent system of in spection and grant of recognition or de -
recognition of institutions pertaining to Indian Systems of Medicine. 
(vii) Produce skilled and professionally competent medical graduates and post -
graduates  
(viii) Place emphasis on substantial evaluation of quality of teaching , training and 
imparting of skills, in addition to assessment of infrastructure and availability of 
human resources in the institutions during inspections.  
 
1.7.4 On 20 th March, 2017, the Committee had drafted the National Commission for Indian 
Systems of Medicine (NCISM) Bill, 2017 and National Commission for Homoeopathy (NCH) 
bill, 2017 on the lines of National Medical Commission Bill, 2016. The said Bills along with 
Preliminary Report of the Committee were uploaded on the website of NITI Aayog on 20 th 
March, 2017 inviting comments from the public. Around 21,987 mails were received from public 
experts (including those who were invited by the Committee) advocacy groups, CC H/CCIM and 
State.  
1.8 The Government of India meanwhile undertook a landmark step on the Modern Medicine 
front and introduced the National Medical Commission Bill, 2016 to revamp the Indian Medial 
Council Act, 1956. The said Bill included several far -reaching changes for strengthening the 
regulation of the medical education in the country. Given the fact that a number of issues 
plaguing MCI were also the ones affecting the CCIM, the NITI Ayog Committee recommended 
for enactment of the National Commission f or Indian System of Medicine on the same lines as 
that of the National Medical Commission Bill, 2016. 
1.9 The Government of India introduced the National Medical Commission Bill, 2017 on the 
29th December, 2017 and referred to the Committee on Health and F amily Welfare on the 4 th 
January, 2018. The Committee presented its 109 th Report on the said Bill on 28 th March, 2018 
containing a total of 56 recommendations.  The Government has accepted a total of 40 
recommendations of the DRSC on Health and Family Welf are, 7 were partially accepted and 9 
recommendations were not accepted.  The National Medical Commission is in place now after 

7 
 
enactment of the National Commission Act, 2019 (No. 30 of 2019 with effect from 8 th August, 
2019). As the NMC Act replaced the IM C Act, 1956, on the same lines the Ministry of AYUSH 
has proposed to supersede the Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 1970 vide the National 
Commission for Indian System of Medicine Bill, 2019.  The National Commission for Indian 
System of Medicine, Bill 2019 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 2 nd January, 2019 and 
referred to the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family 
Welfare on the 14th January, 2019 for examination and report.    
1.10 Salient Features of the Natio nal Commission for Indian System of Medicine, Bill 
2019. 
 The salient features of the National Commission for Indian Systems of Medicine 
(NCISM) Bill, 2019 may be enumerated as under:- 
1.10.1  Institutional Framework for Regulation of Medical Education 
 The Bill proposes constitution of a Commission, in the form of a National Commission 
for Indian System of Medicine, an Advisory Council for Indian System of Medicine and four 
Autonomous Boards for regulating all aspects relating to standard of medical educat ion, 
professionals and institutions in the Indian System of Medicine. 
1.10.2  Composition and Structure of National Commission for Indian Systems of 
Medicine (NCISM) Bill, 2019  
(i) The National Medical Commission comprises of a Chairperson, twelve ex -officio 
members and sixteen part-time members.  
(ii) Of the sixteen part-time members, four Members will be appointed from amongst 
persons of ability, integrity and standing, who have sp ecial knowledge and 
professional experience in any of the disciplines of Indian System of Medicine, 
Sanskrit, Management, Law, Health Research, Science and Technology and 
Economics. Six Members will be appointed on rotational basis from amongst the 
nominees of the States and Union territories in the Advisory Council for Indian 
System of Medicine for a term of two years. Three Members will be elected by 
the registered medical practitioners of Ayurveda, and one member each to be 
elected by the respective regi stered medical practitioners of Siddha, Unani and 
Sowa-Rigpa, of the Indian System of Medicine, from amongst themselves, from 
such regional constituencies and in such manner, as may be prescribed.  
(iii) The Central Government is empowered to appoint the Chairperson, three part -
time members and the Secretary of the Commission, on the recommendation of a 
Search Committee. The Bill also provides for the qualifications for appointment 
of Chairperson, part -term members and Secretary along with the manner of th eir 
appointment. 

8 
 
1.10.3  Autonomous Boards under the National Commission for Indian Systems of 
Medicine: 
 Under the overall supervision of the Commission, four Autonomous Boards will be 
constituted. The Central Government will appoint the President and Mem bers of these 
Autonomous Boards on the basis of the recommendations made by a Search Committee. Every 
Autonomous Board shall meet at least once a month at such time and place as it may appoi nt. 
The brief outline of the composition, powers and functions of these Boards is as follows:- 
(i)  The Board of Ayurveda 
The Board of Ayurveda will consist of a President and four Members from the Ayurveda 
discipline of Indian System of Medicine. The Board will determine the standards of education 
and frame guidelines for setting up of medical institutions at the undergraduate, postgraduate and 
super-speciality levels in Ayurveda discipline.  
(ii)  The Board of Unani, Siddha and Sowa-Rigpa 
The Board of Unani, Siddha and Sowa -Rigpa shall consist of a President and two 
Members from each of the Unani, Siddha and Sowa -Rigpa disciplines of Indian System of 
Medicine. The Board will determine the standards of education and frame guidelines for setting 
up of medical institutions at the undergraduate, postgraduate and super -speciality levels in 
Unani, Siddha and Sow-Rigpa discipline.  
(iii)  The Medical Assessment and Rating Board for Indian System of Medicine 
The Medical Assessment and Rating Board for Indian System of Medicine shall consist 
of a President and eight Members, provided that the President and six out of eight Members shall 
be chosen from the Ayurveda, Siddha, Sowa -Rigpa and Unani disciplines of Indian System of 
Medicine in such manner that at least one Member represents each such discipline separately, 
and the remaini ng two Members be chosen from any of the disciplines of management, quality 
assurance, law or science and technology. 
 The Medical Assessment and Rating Board for Indian System of Medicine shall perform 
the following functions, namely:––  
(a) determine the procedure for assessment and rating of medical institutions on the 
basis of their compliance with the standards laid down by the Board of Ayurveda 
or, as the case may be, the Board of Unani, Siddha and Sowa -Rigpa, in 
accordance with the regulations made under this Act; 
(b)  grant permission for establishment of a new medical institution in accordance 
with the provisions of section 29;  
(c)  carry out inspections of medical institutions for assessing and rating such 
institutions in accordance with the regulations made under this Act: 

9 
 
(d)  conduct, or where it deems necessary, empanel independent rating agencies to 
conduct, assess and rate all medical institutions, within such period of their 
opening, and every year thereafter, at such time, and in such manne r, as may be 
specified by regulations;  
(e)  make available on its website or in public domain, the assessment and ratings of 
medical institutions at regular intervals, in accordance with the regulations made 
under this Act;  
(f)  take such measures, inclu ding issuing warning, imposition of monetary penalty, 
reducing intake or stoppage of admissions and recommending to the Commission 
for withdrawal of recognition, against a medical institution for its failure to 
maintain the minimum essential standards specified by the Board of Ayurveda or, 
as the case may be, the Board of Unani, Siddha and Sowa -Rigpa, in accordance 
with the regulations made under this Act. 
(iv)  The Board of Ethics and Registration for Indian System of Medicine  
The Board shall consist of a  President and eight Members: Provided that the President 
and six out of eight Members shall be chosen from the Ayurveda, Siddha, Sowa -Rigpa and 
Unani disciplines of Indian System of Medicine. The Board of Ethics and Registration for Indian 
System of Medicine shall perform the following functions, namely:––  
(a) maintain a National Register of all licensed practitioners of Indian System of 
Medicine in accordance with the provisions of section 31; 
(b)  regulate professional conduct and promote medical ethics in accordance with the 
regulations made under this Act: Provided that the Board of Ethics and 
Registration for Indian System of Medicine shall ensure compliance with the code 
of professional and ethi cal conduct through the State Medical Council, in a case 
where such State Medical Council has been conferred power to take disciplinary 
actions in respect of professional or ethical misconduct by medical practitioners 
under respective State Acts.  
(c)  develop mechanisms to have continuous interaction with State Medical Councils 
of Indian System of Medicine to effectively promote and regulate the conduct of 
medical practitioners of Indian System of Medicine; 
1.11 National Level Examinations  
The Bill seeks to provide for a statutory basis for the following examinations: 
(i) National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test: The Commission will conduct a common National 
Eligibility cum Entrance Test for admission to the under -graduate courses in each of the 
disciplines of the Indian System of Medicine  
(ii) National Exit Test:  The Commission shall conduct a common final year undergraduate 
medical examination, to be known as the National Exit Test, for granting licence to practice as 

10 
 
medical practitioner of respective disciplines of Indian System of Medicine and for enrolment in 
the State Register or National Register. 
(iii) Post-Graduate National Entrance Test:  The Commission shall conduct a uniform Post -
Graduate National Entrance Test for admission to postgraduate course s in each discipline of the 
Indian System of Medicine in all medical institutions governed under this Act. 
(iv) National Teachers Eligibility Test for Indian System of Medicine: The Commission shall 
conduct a National Teachers’ Eligibility Test for the pos tgraduates of each discipline of Indian 
System of Medicine who desire to take up teaching profession in that discipline.

2.1.5   The Ministry informed the Committee that the proposed National Commission for 
Indian System of Medicine is expected to assess the requirements in healthcare including human 
resources for health and healthcare infrastructure and develop a roadmap and to lay down 
policies for meeting such requirements.

(a) Conducting a common National Eligibility -Cum-Entrance Test and common counselling 
by the designated authority(Central and State) for admission to all the medical institutions 
so as to ensure quality and transparency in admissions.  
(b) Conducting a National Exit Test for granting licence to practice as medical practitioner of 
respective disciplines of Indian System of Medicine and for enrolment in the State 
Register or National Register. 

14 
 
(c) Uniform Post -Graduate National Entrance Test shall be conducted separately for 
admission to postgraduate courses in each discipline of the Indian System of Medicine in 
all medical institutions. 
(d) Conducting National Teachers Eligibility Test fo r appointment of all teachers in Indian 
System of Medicine institutions before their appointment to ensure quality of teachers.  
2.1.7   The National Commission for Indian System of Medicine through its autonomous 
Board, namely, the Board of Ethics and Reg istration for Indian System of Medicine shall ensure 
that the practice in Indian System of Medicine is allowed only by the licensed practitioners so as 
to promote equitable and universal Healthcare through ISM mode of treatment. The Board also 
regulates pr ofessional conduct and promotes medical ethics through State Medical Councils. 
Under the Act, the practice of Indian System of Medicine shall be regulated uniformly across the 
country.

under respective State Acts.
